NestSync

A mobile app that helps roommates share chores, split bills, plan meals, coordinate moods, and manage their home — without the awkward conversations.

The story in six decisions

Designing for the coordination people feel—but rarely name.

Problem

Roommates were spreading chores, bills, meals and emotional check-ins across separate apps and conversations. The real problem was not task completion; it was shared visibility.

Discovery

Research with 42 users showed that coordination breaks down when responsibility is implied. People needed one trusted view of who is doing what and what still needs attention.

Assumption I changed

I initially planned a shared shopping cart. Users already had places to buy things; they needed agreement around what to buy. I removed commerce and focused on coordination.

Key trade-off

An “everything app” could easily become overwhelming. I traded maximum feature density for four clearly separated areas and a home view that surfaces only the next useful action.

Solution

NestSync brings chores, shared spending, meals and household mood into one mobile system with visible ownership, quick updates and a calmer home-level overview.

Outcome + next step

The work produced a research-backed information architecture and 300+ screens. Next, I would test notification load and long-term household adoption with a smaller functional pilot.

Project Overview

One app for
everything shared

NestSync unifies five core pain points of shared living — chore management, expense splitting, meal planning, household communication, and event planning — into a single, coherent mobile experience.

I owned this project end-to-end over 8 months: from initial interviews and card sorting sessions through information architecture, paper wireframes, user flows, and 300+ high-fidelity screens across 10 feature modules — designed in Figma and Adobe Illustrator.

The Problem

Shared living is
fragmented by design

Roommates juggle 4–6 separate apps to manage daily shared life — WhatsApp for chat, Splitwise for money, Todoist for chores, Google Calendar for plans. Nothing integrates. Frustration builds silently until it doesn't.

Chore conflicts
No shared visibility on who's doing what. Verbal agreements fail when nobody tracks follow-through.
Money awkwardness
Asking housemates to pay back is uncomfortable. Expenses get forgotten, disputed, or ignored.
Zero shared context
Nobody knows if someone is home, busy, or having a bad day until they physically walk in.
Lost house rules
House agreements and lease documents live in WhatsApp scroll — impossible to find when needed.
How Might We

Design one unified app that makes shared living feel calm, coordinated, and conflict-free — without adding friction to everyday life?

User Personas

Four voices.
One product.

Four research-backed personas shaped the product decisions — from accountability and fairness to low-effort reminders, grocery visibility, and calmer roommate communication.

Revathi Chinmayi
22 · Part-time employee & student · Kansas
Pain-focused
  • Needs predictable reminders because verbal chore agreements are often forgotten
  • Wants one place for chores, shared costs, and household updates
  • Struggles with duplicate groceries and food expiring in the fridge
  • Prefers gentle nudges instead of repeated group-chat reminders

“I need one calm place that tells me what is pending without making me chase everyone.”

Navya
23 · Graduate student + part-time employee · Rolla, MO
Fairness-focused
  • Wants visible task ownership so responsibilities feel fair
  • Needs proof of completed chores without creating arguments
  • Gets frustrated when groceries are bought twice or wasted
  • Needs shared rules and reminders that everyone can see

“I don’t want to be the house manager. I just want everyone to see the same responsibilities.”

Tarun Kalivarapu
19 · Undergraduate student · Shared apartment
Simplicity-focused
  • Prefers simple checklists over detailed setup screens
  • Needs quick actions: view task, mark done, ask for help
  • Responds better to friendly reminders than strict warnings
  • Wants expense and chore updates to take less than a minute

“Just show me what I need to do today and make it easy to finish it.”

Priya Raghavan
25 · Early-career professional · Austin, TX
Planner-focused
  • Plans ahead and wants household routines to stay consistent
  • Has tried spreadsheets, but housemates stop updating them
  • Needs meal planning, pantry, and bills connected in one flow
  • Wants contribution insights without sounding confrontational

“I want structure that feels easy enough for everyone to actually keep using.”

The Design

Feature by
feature

From paper sketches to high-fidelity Figma screens — every interaction designed with purpose, grounded in research, and tested with real users across 8 months of iteration.

Wireframing

Paper first,
pixels second

Every screen was sketched on paper before opening Figma. This constraint forced faster decision-making — layout choices at lo-fi speed, without the friction of design tools getting in the way of thinking.

Seven modules, 40+ paper wireframes, covering every flow from chore assignment to expense settlement. The sitemap was validated through card sorting before a single frame was opened in Figma.

Paper wireframes for all 7 modules before any digital work
Card sorting with 3 users validated the IA before hi-fi began
20+ user flows mapped every edge case and decision point

Digital Wireframes

Lo-fi to hi-fi — every screen mapped

Before applying any visual design, every screen was built as a digital wireframe in Figma — grayscale layouts establishing information hierarchy, spacing, and interaction patterns across all 10 modules.

Prototyping

From lo-fi
to high-fidelity

After wireframes were validated, I moved into Figma for lo-fi digital screens, then progressively applied the NestSync design system — purple + yellow palette, Poppins typography, custom illustration assets created in Adobe Illustrator.

The final prototype covers 300+ screens across 10 modules with fully linked navigation flows — clickable in Figma, tested with 5 users across 3 rounds of usability testing.

Lo-fi

Hi-fi

Adobe
Illustrations & assets in Adobe Illustrator · icons · onboarding art
01

Onboarding

A welcoming first impression

Three illustrative onboarding slides communicate NestSync's promise before any login wall — "Stay on top of chores", "Plan together, stress less", "Stay connected". Sign-up requires only Name + Email + Password, with Google, Facebook, and Apple social auth as alternatives.

Email verification is handled through a clean OTP card with an animated illustration — "Check your mail ✨" — keeping trust-building entirely on-brand.

02

Household Setup

Create or join in seconds

After login, users either create a new household — which auto-generates a unique code (e.g. RM4821) and QR — or join an existing one via code or QR scan. The household becomes the shared workspace for every feature.

Members can always be invited later from Household Settings. The management hub centralises roommate viewing, rule organization, and leaving flows in one accessible screen.

03

Home Dashboard

Your household at a glance

The home screen is the command centre. Daily Summary surfaces the most urgent tasks above the fold. Sticky Notes render housemate messages inline. The floating yellow + FAB handles all creation without cluttering navigation.

Top-right shortcuts give instant access to Vibe (mood) and House Hold. Bottom nav keeps all five modules thumb-reachable: Home · TaskSync · Kitchen · SplitBills · Profile.

04

TaskSync

Chores assigned,
tracked, and done

TaskSync is the chore module born directly from the #1 pain point in research. Tasks include category, priority badge, due date, assignee avatar, reminder frequency, and an "Ask for Help" escalation flow.

The Remark Box enables async per-task comments. Swipe to mark complete triggers a confirmation modal with time log saved — closing the feedback loop transparently for all housemates.

05

Kitchen

Shared meals, organized

Survey data showed 46% of respondents lose or waste food items regularly. Kitchen addresses this with collaborative meal planning, a shared grocery list with per-item assignment, and pantry/fridge inventory with expiry tracking.

Expiring Soon alerts surface perishables before they're lost. Every item shows who added, edited, or removed it — creating gentle accountability without confrontation.

06

SplitBills

Money without the awkwardness

60% of survey respondents use Splitwise but still face tracking gaps. SplitBills integrates expense splitting within the household context — no switching apps, no lost context.

Equal or custom split, receipt photo uploads, recurring payments for rent and utilities, and one-tap settlement flows make the "can you pay me back?" conversation unnecessary.

07

Vibe — Mood & Planorama

Emotional intelligence
for shared living

The feature almost cut for scope — and the most discussed in every usability test. 71% of surveyed users explicitly wanted to know their housemate's mood before interacting.

Vibe broadcasts emoji + location + availability. Planorama handles event creation with RSVP states: Joining / Not Joining / Confused — rendered as stacked avatar piles that make response status immediately scannable.

Sticky Notes · Rules · Blocking

The supporting cast

Sticky Notes give housemates a targeted, visual way to leave reminders without flooding group chats. Notes are sent to specific recipients and appear on their dashboard home screen.

Rules & Documents centralises house agreements and PDFs — no more digging through WhatsApp scroll. Blocking provides privacy-first protection for difficult living situations, with transparent consequence communication before any action is confirmed.

Design Decisions

The why
behind the what

Every visual and interaction choice was grounded in research, validated in testing, and refined across multiple iterations.

01
Yellow + Purple palette
Yellow (#F5E9C8) signals warmth and home; purple (#7877BA) communicates trust and coordination. Together they feel energetic without aggression — right for daily domestic use.
02
Illustration-led empty states
Custom illustrations turn empty states into invitations, not failures. Consistent style across all 10 modules reinforces brand personality and reduces new-user anxiety.
03
Card-based architecture
All content lives in cards — tasks, events, bills, notes. Supports scalability, scannability, and a consistent interaction model. Adding more items never breaks the layout.
04
Household as the unit
All features are scoped to the household, not the individual. This enables real-time shared context, makes the product sticky, and mirrors how roommates actually think about their home.
05
3-state RSVP
Joining / Not Joining / Confused constrains options to reduce cognitive load, enables stacked avatar visualisation, and eliminates passive non-responses that create planning uncertainty.
06
Bottom nav + FAB
Five-item bottom nav keeps all destinations thumb-reachable. The floating yellow + FAB accelerates creation without cluttering navigation — consistent, platform-native, instantly learnable.

Reflections

What I
took away

Design systems save 10× time
Building a component library early meant Screen 300 was as consistent as Screen 3. In daily-use apps, inconsistency destroys trust quietly.
Research before assumptions
I planned a "shared shopping cart." Research revealed users had Amazon for that — they needed coordination around what to buy, not the buying itself.
Emotion drives retention
Vibe was almost cut for scope. User testing showed it was the most-discussed feature. Emotional visibility reduces conflict better than any task management flow.
IA is the hardest part
Where household settings live took three iterations. Card sorting upfront — validated with real users — would have saved significant rework in Figma and Illustrator.

A product built from real research, designed to last.
